title: Surreal bound for the Riemann hypothesis: why $\delta = 0$ on the critical line
html:
Remark. Surreal bound for the Riemann hypothesis: why \delta = 0 on the critical line

The classical Riemann hypothesis states that every non-trivial zero \rho of the Riemann zeta function satisfies \mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2 (Riemann hypothesis). We express the QOU stability argument for this claim as a literal surreal inequality.

Let \varepsilon \in \mathrm{Der}(A) be the Reeb infinitesimal (Reeb infinitesimal), so that q = 1 + \varepsilon (q from \varepsilon). The scaling laws of surreal rate calculus hold:

\Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3, \qquad \Omega_q \asymp \varepsilon^{-1}.

Let \rho be a hypothetical zero of \zeta(s) with \mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2 + \delta for some \delta \in \mathbb{R}, \delta > 0. We call \delta the rogue-zero drift.

By collapse of the quantum gap and the Hasse--Weil alignment at every prime fibre, the energy required to relocate a zero from \mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2 to \mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2 + \delta is

E(\delta) \asymp \delta^2 \cdot \Omega_q \asymp \delta^2 \cdot \varepsilon^{-1},

while the available dissipation from the mass gap is \Delta_q \asymp \varepsilon^3. Therefore

\frac{E(\delta)}{\Delta_q} \asymp \frac{\delta^2 \cdot \varepsilon^{-1}}{\varepsilon^3} = \delta^2 \cdot \varepsilon^{-4} \qquad (\text{in } \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon) \subset \mathbf{No}).

By surreal squeeze, \delta^2 \cdot \varepsilon^{-1} > \varepsilon^3 in \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon) whenever \delta > 0 is a standard real. Equivalently, \ordw\bigl(E(\delta)\bigr) = 1 > -3 = \ordw(\Delta_q) in the \omega-adic order of Big-O via \ordw: the cost sits at strictly higher \omega-order than the budget.

No configuration of the QOU substrate can sustain a standard-real drift \delta > 0. The only value of \delta with E(\delta) \leq \Delta_q in the ordered field is \delta = 0, i.e., \mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2. This realizes, at the level of surreal arithmetic, the equivalence macroscopic stability \Leftrightarrow RH.

The informal bound "as q \to 1^+, the energy cost O(\delta^2 (q-1)^{-1}) exceeds the closing mass gap O((q-1)^3)" becomes a single inequality \delta^2 \cdot \varepsilon^{-1} > \varepsilon^3 inside the ordered field \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon) \subset \mathbf{No}. No limit is taken; the argument is algebraic, not analytic.

The phrase "almost everywhere on the critical line" in classical partial-RH results corresponds to the standard part \mathrm{st}(\delta) = 0 of a surreal-valued drift—a genuine, not asymptotic, vanishing. This bound upgrades this to \delta = 0 on the nose for any standard real \delta > 0, using only the ordering of \mathbb{R}(\varepsilon).
